topic: Transistor as a Switch and an Amplifier
title: Transistor: Switch or Amplifier? Explained Simply | PUC Electronics
description:
Aarav whispers into a microphone and the speakers boom. A street lamp switches on by itself at dusk. Two very different jobs, one tiny part: the transistor. We start with a water tap (a small twist controls a big flow), then meet the base, collector and emitter of an npn transistor.

On a live breadboard the input flips from 0 V to 5 V: the lamp goes from dark (cut-off) to fully on (saturation) while the oscilloscope shows the output going low when the input goes high. Then we bias it half on, add a tiny 10 mV wave, and watch a big, upside-down wave come out: a common emitter amplifier. The output against input graph shows the three regions, then we derive I_E = I_B + I_C, I_C = beta I_B, V_out = V_CC - I_C R_C and the voltage gain A_v = -beta R_C / R_in. A worked example checks whether a transistor is saturated, followed by the exam trap (the CE output is 180 degrees out of phase, and the extra power comes from the supply), where it is asked, an original practice question with a full solution, and a formula card to screenshot.

This is Episode 50 of PUC Electronics, Class 11, Chapter 7: Bipolar Junction Transistor (Karnataka I PUC Electronics). Transistors are no longer in the rationalised NCERT/CBSE Class 12 Physics book or the current ISC Physics syllabus, so this lesson follows the Karnataka PUC Electronics syllabus.
